strengths: Novel dataset contribution: FrameOracle-41K is the first large-scale VideoQA dataset with explicit keyframe annotations, filling a genuine gap in existing resources
Comprehensive evaluation: Demonstrates broad applicability across 5 VLMs and 6 diverse benchmarks (both long-form and short-form video understanding)
Practical impact: Achieves 35-39% frame reduction while maintaining or improving accuracy; latency reduced by ~40%
Plug-and-play design: Works with different VLMs without co-training or backbone-specific adaptation
Interesting finding (RQ1): Well-demonstrated evidence that more frames don't always improve performance, with supporting qualitative examples
Thoughtful dataset creation: Two-stage pipeline with cross-model verification (3 independent VLMs) adds robustness
Clear presentation: Well-organized paper with good figures, comprehensive appendices, and implementation details
weaknesses: Dataset quality concerns: FrameOracle-41K uses automated pipeline (agent + verification) without human annotation; no inter-annotator agreement or human evaluation of ground truth minimal frames
Limited methodological novelty: FrameOracle uses standard components (Transformer encoders, RankNet loss, categorical heads); individual techniques are well-established
Incomplete analysis: Missing explanation for Stage 1 underperformance (Table 4), no failure case analysis, no investigation of why MLVU improvements are smaller
LOO approach not thoroughly evaluated: Leave-one-out training signal in Stage 2 is computationally expensive and potentially noisy, but reliability not discussed
Lack of statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple random seeds; some improvements are modest (1-2%)
Reproducibility barriers: Relies on proprietary APIs (Qwen2.5-VL-72B), requires 8×H100 GPUs with 40-90 hour training per stage, no code/dataset release announced
Limited generalization: Evaluated only on VideoQA; transferability to other video tasks (summarization, action recognition) unexplored; dataset bias unknown
Parameter justification missing: λk = 0.0105 penalty in Stage 3 and filtering threshold λ in dataset creation appear empirically chosen without sensitivity analysis
Insufficient error analysis: No characterization of linguistic/temporal patterns driving frame count predictions; missing analysis of which question types benefit most
High computational cost of dataset creation not discussed: Expense of agent API calls for ~100K videos is non-trivial and limits reproducibility

strengths: Valuable dataset contribution: FrameOracle-41K is the first VideoQA dataset with explicit keyframe annotations for minimal sufficient frames, potentially benefiting future research
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 diverse VLMs and 6 benchmarks demonstrating broad applicability and model-agnostic generalization
Well-designed curriculum training progression from weak (SigLIP, leave-one-out) to strong (FrameOracle-41K) supervision, validated by ablations
Practical impact with 39.8% FLOP reduction (16→10.4 frames) while maintaining accuracy across multiple models
Insightful empirical finding (RQ1) that more frames don't always improve performance, supported by qualitative examples
Extensive reproducibility documentation including hyperparameters, training times, prompts, and dataset format
weaknesses: Dataset quality concerns: Agent-based keyframe mining with post-hoc 3-VLM verification lacks human validation; 60% example rejection rate suggests potential selection bias; 'minimal sufficient' is not rigorously defined or validated
Limited methodological novelty: Architecture uses standard components (Transformer + linear projectors + two heads); RankNet loss and categorical K prediction are established techniques

Experimental design issues: K Head manually capped at 16 (contradicting adaptive selection); most benchmarks are multiple-choice (less rigorous); Stage 2 trains on Qwen but evaluates on different VLMs without justified cross-model generalization

Missing critical details: Filtering threshold λ (Stage II) not specified; hyperparameter α in K Head loss (Eq. 3) not provided; no justification for why RankNet loss specifically or why this curriculum order is optimal

Severe generalization limitations: Evaluation limited to VideoQA task family; truly long-form videos (1+ hours) not tested despite motivation; 'plug-and-play' claim overstated (training uses specific Qwen tokenizer and DINOv2 encoder)

Presentation issues: Figure formatting error (two 'Figure 1' captions on page 3); inconsistent terminology for 'keyframes'; inadequate ethics section (acknowledges biases but provides no analysis or mitigation)

strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: adaptive frame selection for efficient video-language understanding with plug-and-play applicability across diverse VLMs

Introduces FrameOracle-41K, the first VideoQA dataset with explicit keyframe annotations specifying minimal sufficient frames—a valuable community resource with 40,992 annotated examples and thoughtful cross-model verification

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 VLMs and 6 benchmarks (mix of short and long-form tasks) with thorough ablations, computational analysis (FLOPs, latency, tokens), and comparisons to SOTA methods
Strong empirical findings with consistent results: 35% frame reduction (16→10.4) with no accuracy loss; 64→13.9 frames with +1.4% accuracy improvement across diverse models
Well-motivated four-stage curriculum learning approach progressing from weak (SigLIP alignment) to strong (FrameOracle-41K) supervision is pedagogically sound
Insightful observation (RQ1) that additional frames don't guarantee better performance—contradicts intuition and supported by convincing qualitative examples (Figures 5-6)

Technically sound architecture with clean design (cross-modal fusion + dual prediction heads) and strong reproducibility: comprehensive implementation details, hyperparameters, training times, dataset format provided
weaknesses: Dataset creation relies on single-model mining (Qwen2.5-VL-72B only) creating potential representational bias; Stage II's strict requirement for all 3 models to agree may exclude harder cases or introduce selection bias toward easier examples; no inter-annotator agreement metrics or reliability analysis of agent relevance scores used as training targets

Limited conceptual novelty: core contributions combine standard techniques (RankNet ranking, LOO importance estimation, cross-modal fusion); jointly predicting frame importance and count is incremental rather than fundamental advance

Training/backbone bias: Stages 2-3 train using Qwen2.5-VL-3B as backbone VLM—may introduce model-specific bias despite plug-and-play claims; generalization to video tasks beyond VideoQA (action recognition, detection) unexplored

Mixed benchmark-specific results: FrameOracle underperforms on MLVU (62.9 vs KFC's 63.0, Table 2); no analysis of which task characteristics favor/penalize the approach; missing comparisons on some benchmarks

Design choices lack full justification: (1) Stage 1 performs worse than random baseline despite claimed foundational value; (2) hard cap at K=16 for 64-frame variant unexplained; (3) λ_k=0.0105 appears arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis

Missing critical analysis: no failure case examination, no error distribution over prediction mismatch types, limited architectural ablations (why Transformers vs. simpler fusion?), no analysis of frame selection patterns by question/video type

Experimental concerns: Comparisons with jointly-trained methods use different training data/compute (not entirely fair); filtering threshold λ for dataset Stage II underspecified; dependence on proprietary API (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) may limit reproducibility

Insufficient dataset quality documentation: unclear how many training examples disagreed with ground truth answers, no confidence score distributions from mining stage, limited analysis of annotation consistency across model triplets

strengths: Novel dataset contribution: FrameOracle-41K is the first VideoQA dataset with explicit frame-level annotations specifying minimal sufficient frames per question, with rigorous validation (94% inter-annotator agreement, 93.3% verified accuracy)
Practical plug-and-play design: Model-agnostic frame selector works across diverse VLMs without co-training, addressing a real limitation of prior methods

Comprehensive evaluation: Tested across 5 VLMs and 6 benchmarks with extensive ablation studies validating each training stage; Table 12 conclusively shows gains from semantic selection rather than just fewer frames
Well-motivated four-stage curriculum: Training strategy is thoroughly justified through ablations (Appendix F.1), demonstrating why intermediate weak-supervision stages are necessary
Consistent improvements across diverse models and benchmarks, with clear efficiency-accuracy trade-offs (35-40% frame reduction with maintained or improved accuracy)
Thorough presentation with extensive appendices providing implementation details, additional dataset statistics, human verification protocols, and qualitative examples
weaknesses: Dataset construction bias: FrameOracle-41K uses only LLaVA-Video-178K sources and VLM-dependent filtering (Qwen2.5-VL for mining, three specific VLMs for verification), creating model-dependent bias in 'sufficiency' judgments; ~60% attrition rate (100K→41K) during filtering may systematically remove certain question types
Limited architectural novelty: FrameOracle uses standard components (Transformer encoder, two heads); primary contribution is dataset and problem formulation rather than methodological innovation

Modest accuracy improvements: Many gains are 1-3 percentage points (e.g., NExTQA +1.1); several improvements in Table 1 marked as non-significant (95% CI includes zero); MLVU requires segment-wise workaround, suggesting limitation on very long videos

K head optimization lacks principled justification: Linear penalty λk=0.0105 appears heuristic with no ablation on sensitivity; capping predicted K at 16 when training on 64-frame candidates seems arbitrary; Gaussian soft-target mixing (Eq. 3) not theoretically motivated
No generalization beyond VideoQA: Method trained exclusively on question-answering; transfer to video summarization, action recognition, or other tasks is untested, limiting broader applicability
No error analysis: Missing discussion of failure cases, question types where method struggles, or characteristics of videos where frame selection fails; MLVU underperformance unexplained
High computational training cost: 135-221 GPU-hours per variant (~1000-1700 GPU-hours total on 8 H100s) limits reproducibility and adoption; no cost comparison with baselines

Generalization concerns: Unclear whether dataset bias from model-dependent filtering affects downstream performance; 'minimal sufficiency' is relative to specific VLMs used in verification, not ground truth

strengths: Addresses practical problem of frame selection under computational budgets for VLMs
FrameOracle-41K is a genuine contribution with reasonable annotation quality (94% inter-annotator agreement, 93.3% verified accuracy)
Comprehensive evaluation across 6 benchmarks and 5 VLM backbones demonstrates generalization
Plug-and-play, model-agnostic design without requiring co-training with specific VLMs
Concrete efficiency gains: 35% frame reduction (16→10.4) without accuracy loss
Extensive ablation studies validating multi-stage training curriculum and design choices
Well-structured presentation with clear motivation and thorough experimental details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: architecture is standard (Transformer encoder + two prediction heads); innovation is primarily in dataset, not methodology
Circular dataset construction: dataset created using VLM-based supervision (Stages I-II), then used to train selectors to predict VLM preferences—unclear generalization to future architectures
Narrow evaluation scope: only VideoQA tasks evaluated; unclear if frame selection transfers to video summarization, action recognition, or other video understanding tasks
Multi-stage training complexity without principled justification: why this specific 4-stage curriculum? No comparison with alternative training orderings
Dataset quality concerns: ~7% of annotations potentially problematic (93.3% verified accuracy on 40,992 examples), all filtered using same 3 VLMs introducing architectural bias
Modest improvements: 1-1.5% accuracy gains on long-video benchmarks are modest; inconsistent gains (underperforms SOTA on MLVU with 64 frames)
Insufficient K-head analysis: target K* uses unclear zscore normalization (Eq. 2) with λ_k=0.0105 having no sensitivity analysis; no per-question-type breakdown
Segment-wise extension (Appendix F.4) appears ad-hoc, indicating fundamental limitations with very long videos rather than principled solution
Limited baseline comparisons: difficulty interpreting Table 2 due to different setups; no end-to-end fine-tuning baseline or direct comparison with Video-XL-2
Reproducibility concerns: multi-stage training with dataset-specific hyperparameters, dependency on LLaVA-Video-178K, no mention of code release
Missing generalization analysis: all evaluation on 2-3 minute videos from single source; no domain diversity analysis or robustness to different VLM architectures
Ranking quality only moderate: Kendall-τ of 0.536 indicates selected frames correlate moderately with ground-truth importance, explaining modest improvements

strengths: Novel and well-constructed dataset (FrameOracle-41K): First large-scale VideoQA dataset with keyframe annotations; 93.3% human-verified accuracy with 94% inter-annotator agreement
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Tests on 6 benchmarks across 5 VLMs without co-training; extensive ablations validating all design choices; multiple efficiency metrics reported
Practical and well-motivated problem: Demonstrates that more frames can hurt performance (RQ1); achieves 39.8% FLOP reduction and 41% latency reduction while maintaining/improving accuracy
True plug-and-play generalization: Model-agnostic design works across different VLM architectures without modification or joint training

Principled four-stage curriculum learning: Well-justified progression from weak signals (SigLIP) through proxy supervision (LOO loss) to strong supervision (FrameOracle-41K); ablations confirm necessity of each stage
Honest discussion of limitations and solutions: Acknowledges MLVU challenges and provides segment-wise extension; good academic rigor
Strong human verification and dataset quality: 4,000 samples human-verified; distribution analysis (Figure 6) shows construction process doesn't distort composition
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core architecture is straightforward (standard Transformer encoder + heads); LOO supervision is conventional; main contribution is problem formulation and dataset rather than novel methodology

Dataset sourced from single model and domain: Stage I mining uses only Qwen2.5-VL-72B, potentially introducing model-specific biases; limited to 2-3 min videos from LLaVA-Video-178K; scope doesn't capture diverse real-world scenarios

Questionable experimental design choices: K output capped at 16 for 64-frame model undermines adaptive selection claim; no sensitivity analysis for λ_k=0.0105; imbalanced curriculum (900K→40K samples)
Performance limitations on very long videos: Method doesn't consistently outperform SOTA on MLVU; requires post-hoc segment-wise extension suggesting core approach struggles with extreme lengths

Modest and sometimes non-significant improvements: Many gains in 1-2% range; Table 1 shows several non-significant changes (marked §); some claims of 'no accuracy loss' are actually small improvements within noise

Limited analysis of failure modes and generalization: No per-question-type performance breakdown; failure cases not analyzed; applicability beyond VideoQA (summarization, classification) unclear; only works with uniformly sampled candidates

Reproducibility concerns: No code/dataset release mentioned; heavy dependence on proprietary APIs (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) for dataset generation; while hyperparameters provided, exact reproduction challenging

K Head training instability: Joint Stage 2+3 training causes collapse (Table 10); unclear if fundamental limitation or optimization issue; broader implications for decoupling selection objectives not explored
